sections.h2: What closing costs does a New Jersey seller pay?
sections.html:
Expect one state fee, one possible state surcharge and a handful of private costs. The Realty Transfer Fee lands on the seller at recording, while the buyer carries none of it, and the Division confirms that no sales tax applies to a home sale. Private costs come from your contract and lender, and they vary by deal.

  • The Realty Transfer Fee, a rate times the price shown in the deed.
  • A graduated percent fee when the price tops $1,000,000.
  • Broker compensation, whatever your written agreement says.
  • An estimated income tax deposit if you live outside New Jersey and no exemption fits.
  • The mortgage payoff and any property tax still owed.

Most sellers also supply form RTF-1, the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller. A deed that claims any exemption must carry that affidavit (NJ Division of Taxation).

sections.h2: How is the New Jersey Realty Transfer Fee calculated?
sections.html:
The charge is stacked in slices, with a dollar amount for each $500 and a higher rate for each higher slice of the price. It starts from the price stated in the deed. In a few situations the Division substitutes assessed value divided by the Director's Ratio. Every deed that conveys title is covered unless an exemption fits.

Fee schedule for a standard sale priced above $350,000 (Division of Taxation)
Slice of the priceRate per $500
$0 to $150,000$2.90
$150,000 to $200,000$4.25
$200,000 to $550,000$4.80
$550,000 to $850,000$5.30
$850,000 to $1,000,000$5.80
Above $1,000,000$6.05

A cheaper schedule governs any sale at $350,000 or below, starting at $2.00 per $500 and topping out at $3.90. Stacking those slices on a $325,000 sale yields $1,910, the same answer the Division's FAQ gives. Stacking the table above on a $600,000 sale gives 870, 425, 3,360 and 530, a total of $5,185.

Qualifying seniors, blind or disabled persons and low and moderate income housing use reduced rates. The senior and disability reduction belongs to the person, so an estate or trust cannot claim it.

sections.h2: How does the percent fee on sales above $1 million work?
sections.html:
It is a percentage of the full sale price that the seller owes when consideration passes $1,000,000. Since P.L. 2025, c. 69 took effect on July 10, 2025, the fee is charged to the grantor instead of the buyer. Older descriptions that call it a 1 percent buyer's mansion tax are out of date for deeds submitted on or after that date.

  • 1% of total consideration when the price runs from $1,000,000 up to $2,000,000.
  • 2% when it runs above $2,000,000 up to $2,500,000.
  • 2.5% above $2,500,000 up to $3,000,000.
  • 3% above $3,000,000 up to $3,500,000.
  • 3.5% on prices above $3,500,000.

Each rate is applied to the entire price, so the cost jumps at each threshold instead of building slice by slice. A seller close to a threshold, such as $2,000,000 or $2,500,000, should ask the closing attorney for the exact figure before accepting an offer. The Division's memo works a $2.75 million deed at 2.5 percent, or $68,750 due at recording. It covers Class 2 residential property, farms with a residential building, Class 4A commercial property and cooperative units. A limited refund window applied to deeds above $2 million with contracts fully signed before July 10, 2025 and recorded by November 15, 2025, and that date has passed (Division memo).

sections.h2: Which deeds escape the transfer fee entirely?
sections.html:
The Division lists a long set of full exemptions, and the seller claims one on form RTF-1. Check the facts carefully, because the Division reads each exemption narrowly.

  • Husband and wife, or parent and child, with adopted children counted and stepchildren left out.
  • An executor or administrator passing the house to a named devisee or legal heir.
  • Deeds for consideration under $100.
  • A deed whose only job is to confirm or fix one already on record.
  • Tax sale deeds and deeds on partition.
  • A deed between the divorced spouses filed within 90 days after the decree.

Some transfers look exempt and are not. A sale by an executor to someone who is not named in the will pays the fee. A will that orders a sale and a split of the cash is treated as a gift of money. Moving a house into a trust for other beneficiaries is taxable, and terms of a divorce settlement agreement do not count as specific performance of a judgment. At a sheriff's sale, form RTF-8 is also required, and it is no exemption.

sections.h2: Who sets broker compensation in New Jersey?
sections.html:
You and your brokerage do, in writing. Under P.L. 2024, c. 32, effective August 1, 2024, the brokerage must sign a brokerage services agreement with the seller in every residential transaction. That agreement states the term, the amount of compensation and how it is calculated, and it must say that compensation is fully negotiable and not set by law (DOBI Bulletin 24-11).

  • Compensation may be a flat fee, a percentage of the price or another lawful method.
  • It can be paid by the seller, the buyer, a third party, or shared between brokerages.
  • The agreement must show whether the agency is exclusive or non-exclusive.
  • The brokerage must obtain a signed property condition disclosure statement from the seller.

Showings also changed. At a residential showing open to the public, agents must post a sign saying the agent represents the seller and that what a visitor tells the agent is not confidential. If you hold your own open house through a brokerage, expect that sign at the door. Read the agency section before you sign. New Jersey law now recognizes seller's agents, buyer's agents, disclosed dual agents, designated agents and transaction brokers, and each owes you different duties.

sections.h2: Where is the deed recorded, and what if it lands in the wrong county?
sections.html:
A deed is recorded by the clerk of the county containing the parcel. The package includes the RTF paperwork and a GIT/REP form, which the Division describes as two separate requirements handed in at closing. Acceptance is the clerk's decision.

If the package went to the wrong county, record it again in the right one. Form RTF-3 recovers the state share, and the county share needs a separate request to the office that took it by mistake. Have your title agent confirm the county before anything is mailed.

sections.h2: What do two sample New Jersey sales look like in dollars?
sections.html:
Stacking the slices from the schedule makes the numbers concrete. A $450,000 sale pays 870 on the first $150,000, 425 on the next $50,000 and 2,400 on the last $250,000, which totals $3,695 in Realty Transfer Fee. No percent fee applies, because the price stays under $1,000,000.

A $1,200,000 sale shows how the pieces add up. Stacking the fee slices gives 870, 425, 3,360, 3,180, 1,740 and 2,420, or $11,995. The percent fee at the 1 percent tier is $12,000 on the full price, so the two state charges together reach $23,995 before commission, attorney fees or a payoff. These totals come straight from the Division's rate tables and are not a quote for any deal.

A seller living outside New Jersey also faces the estimated tax deposit described on our capital gains page, and that deposit is credited on the later tax return.

faqs.q: Which side of the table owes the transfer fee?
faqs.a: The seller does. Collection happens at recording, and a buyer on an ordinary purchase owes none of it.

faqs.q: Does a house sale carry sales tax?
faqs.a: No, the Division of Taxation says home sales are outside sales tax.

faqs.q: What does the fee run on a $325,000 sale?
faqs.a: It runs $1,910 with no exemption, the figure the Division's FAQ gives for that price.

faqs.q: Does the old mansion tax still fall on buyers?
faqs.a: For deeds submitted on or after July 10, 2025, the seller is responsible for the graduated percent fee on prices above $1,000,000. The rate starts at 1 percent and climbs to 3.5 percent.

faqs.q: Can I negotiate the real estate commission in New Jersey?
faqs.a: Yes. Broker compensation is fully negotiable, not set by law, and must appear in the brokerage services agreement.
